display_name: Lafage, Côtes Catalanes Vieilles Vignes Tessellae
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Sourced from 70-year-old vines in the black schist soils of the Agly Valley, this blend prioritizes the iron-fisted structure of Carignan and Syrah over the fluff of modern fruit-bombs. It is a study in how the Tramontane—a fierce, dry wind from the northwest—concentrates sugars and acidity in the grapes by dehydrating them on the vine.",
  "wine_summary": "Jean-Marc Lafage manages a diverse portfolio across the Roussillon, but the Tessellae Vieilles Vignes is his benchmark for the Côtes Catalanes IGP. By utilizing fruit from the Agly Valley, a corridor defined by dramatic geological upheaval, he focuses on the tension between sun-drenched ripeness and the stark minerality of the soil. This isn't a shy wine; the 14.5% ABV is a direct result of the intense Mediterranean heat trapped by the dark schist stones.\n\nThe blend is anchored by old-vine Carignan, which provides a savory, black-olive depth that younger plantings cannot replicate. Syrah adds a cracked black pepper note and mid-palate weight, while Grenache and Monastrell round out the edges. Unlike many high-alcohol reds from Southern France, this maintains a jagged, stony backbone that keeps the dark fruit from feeling jammy or over-extracted.",
  "terroir_expression": "Black schist—a flaky, slate-like metamorphic rock—dominates the Agly Valley and acts as a thermal heat sink, absorbing sun during the day and radiating it back to the vines at night. This geological feature ensures full phenolic ripeness, resulting in the wine’s deep color and plush texture. The lack of topsoil forces roots deep into the rock fissures, which translates to a distinct iron-like, bloody tang on the finish that cuts through the primary flavors of blackberry and plum.",
  "vinification_summary": "Lafage employs a partial carbonic maceration for the Carignan, a technique where whole clusters are fermented in a CO2-rich environment before crushing. This process creates an enzymatic fermentation inside the berry, extracting vibrant fruit and aromatic precursors while leaving the harsh, aggressive tannins of the Carignan skins behind. The remainder of the blend undergoes traditional fermentation with extended skin contact to ensure the structural integrity required for the 14.5% alcohol to feel balanced rather than hot.",
  "food_pairing": "Pair this with Nashville hot chicken; the wine's residual fruit sweetness and bold body stand up to the cayenne heat without being stripped of flavor. For a classic bistro approach, choose a hanger steak with blue cheese butter, as the wine’s iron notes mirror the mineral profile of the rare meat. At a higher end, serve it with cocoa-rubbed venison to bridge the gap between the wine’s dark fruit and its earthy, savory Carignan base. It also handles casual fare like a pepperoni and black olive pizza, where the saltiness of the toppings highlights the wine's garrigue spice.",
  "comparable_wines": "Domaine Gauby Vieilles Vignes — a more expensive, biodynamic look at the same schist-driven Agly Valley terroir. Saint-Cosme Côtes-du-Rhône — shares the same emphasis on dark fruit and peppery Syrah spice at a similar price point.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry red with rugged tannins and a savory, mineral edge.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink this within five years of the vintage to preserve the primary fruit; store at a constant 55°F to prevent the high alcohol from oxidizing prematurely.",
  "value_assessment": "At roughly $15, this wine consistently punches above its weight, offering more tectonic character than generic $20 Côtes-du-Rhône or mass-market Argentinian Malbec. It is a high-value staple because it provides the concentration of 'old vines' without the prestige markup found in neighboring Languedoc crus. It is a definitive buy for anyone seeking density without spending over $25.",
  "market_position": "This wine serves as the workhorse of serious independent retail shops and savvy glass-pour programs. It appeals to the drinker who wants the power of a Napa Cabernet but prefers the rustic, herbal complexity of Southern France. Collectors will find it too inexpensive to brag about, but it is a reliable 'Tuesday night' bottle for those who value site-specificity.",

parsed.hook: Sourced from 70-year-old vines in the black schist soils of the Agly Valley, this blend prioritizes the iron-fisted structure of Carignan and Syrah over the fluff of modern fruit-bombs. It is a study in how the Tramontane—a fierce, dry wind from the northwest—concentrates sugars and acidity in the grapes by dehydrating them on the vine.
parsed.wine_summary:
Jean-Marc Lafage manages a diverse portfolio across the Roussillon, but the Tessellae Vieilles Vignes is his benchmark for the Côtes Catalanes IGP. By utilizing fruit from the Agly Valley, a corridor defined by dramatic geological upheaval, he focuses on the tension between sun-drenched ripeness and the stark minerality of the soil. This isn't a shy wine; the 14.5% ABV is a direct result of the intense Mediterranean heat trapped by the dark schist stones.

The blend is anchored by old-vine Carignan, which provides a savory, black-olive depth that younger plantings cannot replicate. Syrah adds a cracked black pepper note and mid-palate weight, while Grenache and Monastrell round out the edges. Unlike many high-alcohol reds from Southern France, this maintains a jagged, stony backbone that keeps the dark fruit from feeling jammy or over-extracted.
parsed.terroir_expression: Black schist—a flaky, slate-like metamorphic rock—dominates the Agly Valley and acts as a thermal heat sink, absorbing sun during the day and radiating it back to the vines at night. This geological feature ensures full phenolic ripeness, resulting in the wine’s deep color and plush texture. The lack of topsoil forces roots deep into the rock fissures, which translates to a distinct iron-like, bloody tang on the finish that cuts through the primary flavors of blackberry and plum.
parsed.vinification_summary: Lafage employs a partial carbonic maceration for the Carignan, a technique where whole clusters are fermented in a CO2-rich environment before crushing. This process creates an enzymatic fermentation inside the berry, extracting vibrant fruit and aromatic precursors while leaving the harsh, aggressive tannins of the Carignan skins behind. The remainder of the blend undergoes traditional fermentation with extended skin contact to ensure the structural integrity required for the 14.5% alcohol to feel balanced rather than hot.
parsed.food_pairing: Pair this with Nashville hot chicken; the wine's residual fruit sweetness and bold body stand up to the cayenne heat without being stripped of flavor. For a classic bistro approach, choose a hanger steak with blue cheese butter, as the wine’s iron notes mirror the mineral profile of the rare meat. At a higher end, serve it with cocoa-rubbed venison to bridge the gap between the wine’s dark fruit and its earthy, savory Carignan base. It also handles casual fare like a pepperoni and black olive pizza, where the saltiness of the toppings highlights the wine's garrigue spice.
parsed.comparable_wines: Domaine Gauby Vieilles Vignes — a more expensive, biodynamic look at the same schist-driven Agly Valley terroir. Saint-Cosme Côtes-du-Rhône — shares the same emphasis on dark fruit and peppery Syrah spice at a similar price point.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with rugged tannins and a savory, mineral edge.
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink this within five years of the vintage to preserve the primary fruit; store at a constant 55°F to prevent the high alcohol from oxidizing prematurely.
parsed.value_assessment: At roughly $15, this wine consistently punches above its weight, offering more tectonic character than generic $20 Côtes-du-Rhône or mass-market Argentinian Malbec. It is a high-value staple because it provides the concentration of 'old vines' without the prestige markup found in neighboring Languedoc crus. It is a definitive buy for anyone seeking density without spending over $25.
parsed.market_position: This wine serves as the workhorse of serious independent retail shops and savvy glass-pour programs. It appeals to the drinker who wants the power of a Napa Cabernet but prefers the rustic, herbal complexity of Southern France. Collectors will find it too inexpensive to brag about, but it is a reliable 'Tuesday night' bottle for those who value site-specificity.
parsed.insider_take: Skip this if you demand silkiness; the Carignan here is unashamedly gritty and demands food to show its best side. Most drinkers mistake the ripeness for sweetness, but the finish is bone-dry and driven by a scorched-earth minerality that can be polarizing for those used to polished, oak-driven reds. The real tradeoff is the high alcohol, which requires a slight chill—around 60°F—to keep the heat from overshadowing the floral Syrah notes.
